title: Produce resolved surface maps of rocky exoplanets

concept.text: The innovation is the ability to recover repeatable maps that distinguish multiple locations across the surface of a rocky planet orbiting another star. With sufficient spectral and temporal information, these maps would separate persistent surface structure from changing atmospheric features and artifacts introduced by image reconstruction. The goal is spatially resolved planetary observation, rather than an image whose apparent detail depends on assumptions that the measurements cannot independently test.

Direct multipixel imaging faces severe faintness and angular-resolution challenges. One investigated approach uses the Sun’s gravitational lens to amplify and encode light from an exoplanet, followed by computational reconstruction of its image. This is a possible route to the capability, not part of its definition: another observing architecture could qualify if it delivered comparably convincing maps.

significance.text: Repeatable surface maps would make comparative planetary geography observable on rocky worlds around other stars. The supplied study connects its proposed imaging resolution to observing seasonal changes, oceans, continents and surface topography. If such performance were achieved and validated, researchers could compare spatial structure and its evolution across different planets, substantially extending what can be learned from observations that combine the light of an entire planetary disk.

Conditional scientific implications extend to weather and climate: repeated observations could reveal atmospheric variability and its relationship to persistent surface features, provided the measurements actually distinguish clouds from the underlying surface. A mapped brightness or color pattern would not by itself identify an ocean, a continent, an elevation difference or a weather system. Those interpretations would depend on spectral information, temporal behavior and the reliability of the physical models used to explain the observations.

The capability would be transformative even if none of the mapped planets hosted life. Maps could supply environmental context for investigations under AST-01, “Establish that an exoplanet hosts life,” but a suggestive surface pattern would not establish biology. Similarly, resolving planetary structure would not by itself demonstrate extraterrestrial technology under AST-02. These are conditional downstream opportunities requiring additional evidence, not consequences guaranteed by obtaining a map.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is an observing and reconstruction system that delivers trustworthy spatial information about a rocky exoplanet’s surface. The supplied study identifies the need for substantial light amplification and very high angular resolution. Its solar gravitational lens approach combines optical modeling, instrument design and image reconstruction; the remaining breakthrough requires these elements to work together in an operational observing system rather than only in a technical study.

Engineering synthesis: the system must collect enough useful planetary light, control contaminating light and instrumental effects, and preserve positional and calibration accuracy sufficient to distinguish surface locations. For a solar gravitational lens architecture, the mission must also reach and operate in the required observing geometry and obtain the measurements needed for reconstruction. The supplied abstract does not establish quantitative mission requirements or demonstrate that these operational barriers have been overcome.

Inference synthesis: the reconstruction must show which spatial features are constrained by the measurements and which depend strongly on modeling choices. Changing clouds, illumination and viewing geometry can complicate the separation of atmospheric variability from persistent surface structure. More displayed pixels do not necessarily mean more independently constrained surface elements; uncertainty estimates and tests against reconstruction artifacts are therefore central to demonstrating the capability.

current_state.text: The supplied evidence documents the NASA-funded NIAC Phase II study “Direct Multipixel Imaging and Spectroscopy of an Exoplanet With a Solar Gravity Lens Mission,” by Slava G. Turyshev, Michael Shao, Viktor T. Toth, Louis D. Friedman and Leon Alkalai. The repository metadata gives March 18, 2020 as the publication date and June 27, 2025 as the acquisition date. The later repository date does not make this a 2025 research result.

According to the abstract summarized in the supplied review, the study developed optical models, instrument designs and deconvolution algorithms, and its authors reported the feasibility of high-quality image reconstruction. They characterized the solar gravitational lens imaging and spectroscopy technique as reaching technology readiness level 3. These are reported study achievements and feasibility claims, not a demonstration of an operational system producing resolved surface observations of a rocky exoplanet.

The abstract discusses a proposed configuration involving a 1-m telescope and associates its projected resolution with seasonal changes, oceans, continents and surface topography. These are prospective scientific applications of the modeled capability. The supplied evidence does not independently validate that performance, establish successful weather retrieval, or show that surface and atmospheric contributions have been separated in observations of an actual rocky exoplanet.

The evidence available through the supplied review is the repository landing page’s abstract and metadata. Although that page lists a report download, the full report and its validation details were not inspected in the review. This limits assessment of the authors’ feasibility claims without showing that those claims are false. The supplied material also contains no freshness search establishing the observational frontier as of November 1, 2026; consequently, it cannot support the earlier categorical assertion that no observations currently resolve multiple surface elements on any rocky exoplanet.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: recover repeatable maps with multiple independently constrained surface elements on more than one rocky exoplanet. The observations should include enough spectral and temporal information to distinguish persistent surface structure from clouds and reconstruction artifacts. Using more than one planet would demonstrate an initial comparative capability. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established standards or requirements attributed to the NASA study.
completion_criteria.label: Repeatable independently constrained surface maps across multiple rocky exoplanets

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: independent teams should be able to analyze the observations using documented calibration, uncertainty estimates and reconstruction methods. Features should remain supported across reasonable changes in reconstruction assumptions and recur consistently in observations where the viewing conditions permit comparison. Tests using known synthetic scenes, deliberate searches for false features and repeat observations would help establish which recovered spatial information is reliable. Success on simulations alone would not complete the proposed observational demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Independent analyses reproduce observed features across reasonable reconstruction assumptions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report the effective spatial resolution and number of independently constrained elements, spectral coverage, observing cadence, integration time, uncertainty and sensitivity to atmospheric obscuration. Demonstrations should state the target distances, brightnesses and viewing conditions over which the method works, and distinguish broad persistent regions from finer geographic or topographic claims. Finite observations would establish demonstrated breadth across the tested planets and conditions, not universal applicability to every rocky exoplanet.
completion_criteria.label: Report spatial resolution, observational requirements and demonstrated operating limits

related_concepts.text: AST-01, “Establish that an exoplanet hosts life,” has the closest scientific overlap: resolved maps could provide environmental context and locate features for further investigation. Its evidentiary endpoint remains distinct, because mapping geography or atmospheric variability does not establish life. AST-02, “Detect an independently verifiable extraterrestrial technology,” could likewise benefit from spatial context, but identifying technology would require evidence beyond a resolved surface pattern. These relationships are synthesis based on the supplied roster titles.

AST-06, “Map the cosmic dark ages and first luminous structures in three dimensions,” shares the broad ambition of recovering spatial information that is difficult to observe. Its targets and endpoint differ: cosmic structures in three dimensions versus surface structure on individual rocky exoplanets. AST-09, “Make neutrino astronomy capable of routinely resolving hidden cosmic sources,” and AST-10, “Open the millihertz gravitational-wave sky as a working observatory,” share an emphasis on enabling an observational capability, but concern different messengers and source populations.

AST-07, “Discover a reproducible breakdown of general relativity near black holes,” has a limited conceptual connection through gravitational physics. Using the Sun as a gravitational lens is an imaging technique; it would not itself establish a breakdown of general relativity near black holes. The remaining supplied entries—AST-03, AST-04, AST-05, AST-11, AST-12, AST-13 and AST-14—address different constituents, cosmic histories or physical mechanisms. The supplied material establishes no direct dependency between their completion and rocky-exoplanet surface mapping.

brief.title: Reliable surface maps of worlds around other stars
possible: We could compare the geography of rocky planets around other stars. Repeatable maps would distinguish lasting surface regions from passing clouds and follow how those regions change with the seasons.
why: Astronomers could study differences between places on a distant world, beyond what its combined light reveals. Maps would let them compare planetary geography and investigate how weather and climate relate to the surface.

sources.showed: They developed telescope designs and image reconstruction methods for using the Sun’s gravity to focus a distant planet’s light. Their study reported that detailed imaging was feasible.
sources.quote: We developed deconvolution algorithms and demonstrated the feasibility of high-quality image reconstruction.
sources.cited_for: The Sun’s gravity offers a possible route to detailed planetary maps.
sources.not_established: The study did not demonstrate an operating mission mapping a rocky planet around another star.

sources.showed: They inferred a rocky planet’s heat distribution from its changing infrared brightness. The map showed a strong contrast between day and night.
sources.quote:
revealing highly asymmetric dayside thermal emission and 
a strong day–night temperature contrast.
sources.cited_for: Changing total brightness can reveal broad differences between regions of a rocky planet.
sources.not_established: The heat pattern could reflect an atmosphere or surface magma flows; it does not establish persistent surface geography.

sources.showed: They combined Earth’s light into a single point and reconstructed a surface map from changes in brightness and color. They recovered the major continents, with errors over oceans.
sources.quote:
We present the first 
two-dimensional (2D) surface map of Earth reconstructed from light curve observations 
without any assumptions of its spectral properties.
sources.cited_for: Earth observations demonstrate that combined planetary light contains recoverable geographic information.
sources.not_established: This was a test using Earth, and persistent clouds could still be confused with surface features.

sources.showed: In a preprint, they recovered broad surface patterns from simulated observations with changing clouds. Applied to Earth observations, their method removed little cloud cover.
sources.quote:
When applied to observations from
the Earth Polychromating Imaging Camera aboard the DSCOVR spacecraft, our approach
removesonlyasmallfractionofclouds.
sources.cited_for: Cloud removal can succeed in simulations while remaining difficult with real observations.
sources.not_established: The method did not demonstrate reliable separation of clouds and surface features on a planet around another star.

sources.showed: Webb telescope observations matched a rocky planet that reflects almost no light and carries little heat to its night side.
sources.quote:
all fully consistent with a zero-albedo
planet with no heat recirculation.
sources.cited_for: Heat measurements can constrain broad day–night differences and possible atmospheres on rocky planets.
sources.not_established: These measurements provide little information about surface composition and do not establish a repeatable geographic map.

shown: Demory’s team inferred broad heat patterns on a rocky planet around another star. Fan’s team reconstructed Earth’s major continents from its combined light. These results demonstrate pieces of the mapping problem, while cloud separation remains difficult.

Turyshev’s team studied a more detailed imaging approach: using the Sun’s gravity as a lens to focus planetary light. They developed designs and reconstruction methods and reported feasibility, without demonstrating an operating mapping mission.
missing: An operating system must gather enough planetary light and control interference well enough to distinguish surface locations reliably.
Repeat observations must separate lasting surface features from changing clouds and false patterns created during reconstruction.
Maps of multiple rocky planets must contain distinct regions whose features are supported by measurements.

milestones.label: Repeatable surface maps across multiple rocky planets
milestones.explanation: Maps of multiple rocky planets would have to recover distinct surface regions, separating persistent features from clouds and false patterns. This would establish an initial basis for comparing planetary geography.

milestones.label: Independent analyses recover the same observed features
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to recover consistent features from repeat observations under reasonable changes in reconstruction assumptions. This would establish that the measurements support the maps.

milestones.label: Mapping detail, observing needs and limits are measured
milestones.explanation: Demonstrations would have to report reliable map detail, colors measured, timing, observing effort, uncertainty, cloud sensitivity and usable target conditions. This would define which geographic claims the method can support.

uncertain: How reliably can observations distinguish lasting surface regions from persistent clouds and changing illumination?
How much map detail will measurements support independently of reconstruction assumptions?
What accuracy and observing time are sufficient depends on the geographic claim being tested.

page.title: Resolved surface maps of rocky exoplanets
page.definition: Observations yield a two-dimensional image of an Earth-sized rocky planet orbiting another star, resolving surface structure at 10 km scales. The solar gravitational lens—the focusing of light by the Sun’s gravity—is one proposed observing method.

goal.need: The NIAC Phase II study connects 10 km surface resolution with observations of continents, oceans and seasonal changes. For an Earth-sized planet at 30 parsecs, it estimates that conventional imaging at 1 μm requires an aperture of about 90 km even for one resolution element across the disk. Its proposed solar gravitational lens system instead uses a 1 m telescope beyond 548 astronomical units from the Sun.

figures.caption: Imaging requirements estimated in the NIAC Phase II study
figures.note: These are study estimates. The gravitational lens configuration requires an observing spacecraft beyond 548 astronomical units; one astronomical unit is the Earth–Sun distance.

statements.body: NASA Innovative Advanced Concepts, Phase II solar gravitational lens study
statements.quote: with the objective of conducting direct high-resolution imaging and spectroscopy of a habitable exoplanet
statements.context: The proposed study uses the Sun’s gravitational field as an optical lens.

statements.body: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Committee on Exoplanet Science Strategy
statements.quote: image the planetary surface to search for direct signs of habitability, such as the presence of an ocean.
statements.context: The passage describes the scientific purpose of direct imaging of terrestrial planets.

completion.title: Observations recover a rocky exoplanet’s surface image with 10 km spatial resolution.
completion.criterion: Observations of an Earth-sized rocky exoplanet within 30 parsecs recover a two-dimensional surface image with 10 km-scale spatial resolution, meeting the NIAC Phase II study’s imaging target. Resolution concerns recovered surface structure, rather than the number of displayed pixels. The studied implementation uses a 1 m telescope in the solar gravitational lens’s strong-interference region beyond 548 astronomical units from the Sun.
completion.set_by: NASA NIAC Phase II study team, executive summary of its final report dated 18 March 2020; a concept-study performance target, not an approved mission requirement.
completion.threshold_quote: with 10-km scale resolution of its surface
completion.basis: The study explicitly connects this resolution to planetary surface geography. The target and flight milestones belong to the solar gravitational lens concept; they are not a field-wide acceptance standard. A 2026 survey still treats resolved Earth-analogue imaging as an unmet capability. Tests using Earth observations also show that separating clouds from surface structure remains incomplete.

milestones.title: A rocky-exoplanet mapping technology passes NASA’s TRL 3 proof-of-concept test.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate analytical and experimental proof of a critical mapping function, validating predictions through laboratory demonstrations, modelling or simulation. NASA calls this technology readiness level 3. The report dated 18 March 2020 assigns its SGL technique TRL 3. Fan et al. recovered Earth’s major continents from about 10,000 frames over two years. Demory et al. inferred longitudinal thermal emission for 55 Cancri e from 75 h of observations at 4.5 μm in eight visits between 15 June and 15 July 2013; atmospheric and surface explanations remained degenerate.
milestones.set_by: NASA, Technology Readiness Levels table, TRL 3 row; a generic maturity criterion applied to mapping technology. The threshold is stated in the table.

milestones.title: A solar-sail spacecraft demonstrates solar-accelerated flight at 10 astronomical units per year.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a Sun-accelerated solar-sail flight at 10 astronomical units per year and confirm its concept of operations. The NIAC Phase II capability roadmap places this intermediate flight demonstration before the 20 astronomical units per year target-mission launches.
milestones.set_by: NASA NIAC Phase II study team, final report, section 5.8, page 74; this demonstration is specific to its solar-sail mission architecture.

milestones.title: The complete surface-mapping observatory passes NASA’s TRL 8 flight-qualification test.
milestones.criterion: The observatory in its final configuration passes test and analysis for its intended operational environment and flight platform. Its reconstruction software is integrated with operational hardware and software, with functionality demonstrated in simulated operational scenarios and verification and validation completed. This is NASA TRL 8.
milestones.set_by: NASA, Technology Readiness Levels table, TRL 8 row; a generic flight-qualification criterion applied to the observatory. The threshold is stated in the table.

milestones.title: An SGL observatory samples exoplanet light at 650–900 AU with position error below 1 m.
milestones.criterion: At 650–900 astronomical units from the Sun, acquire brightness measurements of gravitationally lensed exoplanet light with timestamps and spacecraft positions. Maintain local-reference-frame position error below 1 m and a sampling interval no longer than about 3 minutes, as specified in the mission study’s Table 1. These measurements supply the input for image reconstruction.
milestones.set_by: NASA NIAC Phase III mission study, Helvajian et al., Table 1 and section 3.4; these operating requirements are specific to the solar gravitational lens architecture.
milestones.threshold_quote: This requires a pixel-to-pixel relative navigational accuracy at meter-scale or better.

not_found: No field-wide numerical acceptance test for map fidelity, repeatability or cloud–surface separation was found in the NASA and National Academies material searched.
No published observation meeting the 10 km rocky-exoplanet surface-resolution target was found.

results.finding: One solar gravitational lens imaging technique reached TRL 3.
results.detail: The Phase II study reports modelling and image-reconstruction feasibility for the proposed technique.
results.quote: Under a Phase II NIAC program, we confirmed the feasibility of the SGL-based technique for direct imaging and spectroscopy of an exoplanet, yielding technology readiness level (TRL) of TRL 3.

results.finding: A longitudinal thermal brightness map was inferred for one super-Earth, 55 Cancri e, from 75 hours of observations.
results.detail: The result demonstrates longitudinal mapping, but atmospheric and surface explanations remain possible. The paper does not establish TRL 3 proof through validation of predictions.
results.quote:
Here we report a longitudinal thermal 
brightness map of the nearby transiting super-Earth 55 Cancri e 
(refs 4, 5) revealing highly asymmetric dayside thermal emission and 
a strong day–night temperature contrast.

results.finding: A 2D map of Earth as a proxy exoplanet recovered major continents from 9,740 frames.
results.detail: The frames were integrated into single-point light curves. The reconstruction used known viewing geometry, and its regularization was selected using Earth's known surface map.
results.quote:
Compared with the true land/ocean map (Figure 4b), the retrieved map 
successfully recovers all of the major continents,  while there exist some disagreements over 
oceans.

results.finding: Surface-albedo retrieval recovered low-resolution maps from 30 simulated light curves using eight days of observations.
results.detail: The simulation demonstrated a mapping function under simplified cloud assumptions. The test on eight days of Earth observations produced a poor surface-map approximation because cloud removal was limited.
results.quote:
We ﬁnd that
eight days of continuous synthetic observations are suﬃcient to reconstruct a faithful low
resolutionsurfacealbedomap,withoutneedingtomakeassumptionsaboutcloudphysics.

results.finding: JWST measured the thermal phase curve of one rocky sub-Earth, GJ 367b, over 12.7 hours.
results.detail: The phase curve distinguishes dayside and nightside emission, but does not recover a surface map or establish a mapping technology's TRL 3 status.
results.quote:
Using the Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI; Kendrew et al.
2015) on JWST, we monitored GJ 367b for 12.7 hr,
corresponding to 1.6 planetary orbits (GO 2508; PI: M.
Zhang).

results.finding: Sparse modeling recovered surface features of one Earth analog from two years of simulated observations.
results.detail: The model used Earth observations with injected noise to represent a planet 5 pc away. Recovered maps were compared with Earth's known land map; the optimal parameters were selected using that ground truth.
results.quote:
We ﬁnd that the sparse modeling resolves
Australia, Afro-Eurasia, North America, and South America using 2-year observation with a time
interval of one month.

results.finding: Hybrid spin–orbit tomography recovered Earth-like surface and cloud maps using 512 simulated observation times.
results.detail: The model recovered continental structure from simulated light curves and was also applied to 2,435 Earth observation frames. The authors report remaining surface-component degeneracy and limited spatial resolution. The supplied arXiv version states that the paper was accepted by ApJ and acknowledges a reviewer.
results.quote: Applying the method to a toy Earth model, we successfully recover static surface distributions together with a single time-dependent cloud component.

results.finding: SGL simulation reconstructed Earth’s surface features from about 5,500 simulated observations.
results.detail: The simulation used Earth as a stand-in and assumed known orbital and rotational parameters. Light contamination, unpredictable surface changes and some higher-resolution lens effects were not addressed.
results.quote: We found that after a few thousand samples, taken while the planet rotates, reliable reconstruction of planetary features was possible.

results.finding: An SGL simulation reconstructed spatial contrast from one Earth image at a modeled resolution of 200–230 km.
results.detail: The proof of concept uses a scalar model and assumes calibrated ring extraction. It does not validate physical surface retrieval, a full dynamic inversion, or mission feasibility.
results.quote: propagates it through an aperture-averaged SGL operator, injects individual noise and systematic terms, reconstructs the source with a non-oracle regularized inverse, and quantifies the image degradation introduced by each modeled effect.

results.finding: IKAROS, one solar-sail spacecraft, gained 400 m/s from solar radiation pressure over three years.
results.detail: The source reports solar-accelerated flight but does not establish a speed of 10 astronomical units per year or confirm the milestone's concept of operations.
results.quote: Accelerated by solar radiation pressure, its velocity increment reached 400 m/sec over the three-year flight.
